title: One Knock
text:
The door to apartment 2D was unlocked. That was how he'd left it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood just inside and checked the room. Not for a threat — he knew there was no threat. The kind of check the body runs for you, because eleven years had made it automatic, no thought required. Everything came back the same as always, except the mice.

The lumen mice had moved. Three of them, along the baseboard toward the radiator wall — the wall he shared with <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>, room 2E. He watched them a moment. They ran their new track with the same set purpose they brought to everything. Toward the heat. They didn't explain themselves.

The spot in the alley where the bike always sat was empty. A patch of oil on the concrete, dark and even, the record of a long and steady arrangement. He looked at it a while and then looked away. The bike was gone, and the corner was what it had always been under the bike. Both were true.

He sat down on the floor. Not the bed, not the chair. The floor, which was where you sat when you were done putting things away and not yet ready to start again.

Four facts sat in him. Not as words - words needed time and someone to say them to and some shape of intent, and he had none of those right now. They sat as weight. What he was. What the escape might have been. What the entity had given him at the threshold, whole and untranslated. What it meant that the threshold was gone and the frequency had played its last note. He would carry all four until they found their words. He wasn't going to hurry that.

There was a fifth thing, and it did not sit, because he would not let it. He kept it moving at the edge of the room, where the other four couldn't reach it and press their shape onto it. The last soldier. The one who had been very good. The offer <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had made him at the end — <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> lowered a hand's width, the door held open — and not meant. For eleven years he had meant it every time. He had used the shape of the thing he'd meant for eleven years as a lie, and the lie had bought a half second, and he'd done the rest with his hands. He was done putting things away. He was not going to put that one away. He was going to hold it. It was already true in every way that didn't need words.

He went over the room. The crack in the plaster above the window, eight centimeters, there since year four, spread now to a pale hairline that ran diagonal into the corner, that he'd been meaning to patch for five of the seven years since. Through the glass, south and far, the Thread climbing out of the city on its cargo lights, the one line in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> that never bent. Three lumen mice running the baseboard toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s wall with their small reliable bodies, following a signal he couldn't hear and had never once stopped.

The room asked nothing of him.

That was almost too much.

One knock. Not twice.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard her steps before it — through the shared wall, the exact rhythm he had learned without meaning to in the four years she'd been across the hall. The step-pause-step of someone crossing a workspace without looking down, because she knew the floor by heart. The sound of something set down, then picked back up. Then her door, the hall, the knock.

He got up and opened it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had the soldering iron in her left hand. Not coiled, not capped — warm, the tip pointing down, the way you carry a thing you mean to get back to. She looked at him in the doorway. Her eyes made the trip he was used to: the shoulder, the bandage on his left forearm, the way he was standing. She said nothing about any of it.

"You eat?"

He hadn't.

She turned without waiting for more and went back through her door. He followed.

Her place had its own ordered mess — the workbench with its sorted parts, the workbench with sorted parts she kept at one particular angle, the workbench with sorted parts that had become, without either of them saying so, where he stood when he showed up at this hour in this shape. She was already at the hot plate. He sat on the stool to the left of the worktable, where he always sat.

The iron went into its stand — not tossed, seated, tip clear of the bench the way you leave a live thing so it can't set the sorted parts alight while your back is turned. She didn't unplug it. She never did. She'd told him once that a warm iron re-heated faster than a cold one paid for itself, the way she thought about most things: the small steady cost against the interrupted work.

She didn't ask about the Schism. She didn't ask about <entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">the Gingerbread House</entity> or the <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> soldiers or the four facts he was carrying, still weight and not yet words. He would tell her what she needed to know when there was something she needed to know. She understood that. He understood that she understood it. That was the arrangement. What it was built on top of, neither of them had the words for, or wanted.

She would never ask about the fifth thing. She would never know there was a fifth thing — that there had been a last soldier, what the offer had been, that he had spent it. That was the point. That was what the night had been for: that she could sit here with a warm iron and a man who hadn't eaten, and see the shoulder and the bandage and the way he stood, and never see the rest. He would carry it alone. It was his now — the way the corner had been the bike's, the way the room was his. By long and steady arrangement. No one else's business.

She ladled without measuring, without hesitation, and set the bowl down in front of him. Steam came off it — salt, something green, something that had been bone once, made by someone who had built the heat around the hour he'd arrive and been right. She set the spoon next to it. Not in it. Next to it, where he could choose. Then she took the stool across the worktable with a piece of her own work and did not watch him eat, which was its own kind of watching.

The lamp held its angle. The workbench held its order.

The city needed nothing from him tonight. The broth was hot enough to fog the near edge of the lamp. An arm's length away <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned a housing over under the light, whole, and not knowing.

He picked up the spoon with the hand that still worked right.

He ate.
